Your extracts from [Phase 6](first-extraction.qmd), [Extract from
LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd) and [Phase 11](extract-variables.qmd) are
stored as separate RDS files. Once each extract is down to **one row per
person** ([Long ↔ wide format](long-wide.qmd)), you join them on `pnr` into
one analysis-ready dataset. Finally, you calculate follow-up time and the event
variable.

*Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own.*

::: {.callout-important}
**First get each extract down to one row per person.** `left_join()` only
behaves predictably when both tables have **one row per `pnr`**. Many register
extracts have multiple rows per person (long format). Reduce them to one row per
person with `group_by() + slice()` or `pivot_wider()` - explained in [Long ↔
wide format](long-wide.qmd). This page assumes your extracts are already in
that shape.
:::

## Joins - link two tables {#joins-link-two-tables}

In register-based research you almost always work with data from **two or more
tables** that need to be linked. All joins in `dplyr` take two tables and one
key column they share (e.g. `pnr`).

When you join your **finished person-level extracts onto the cohort**, the key
is usually `pnr`. Inside a register it is other keys: joining contact and
diagnosis in LPR, for instance, happens on `recnum` or `dw_ek_kontakt`, not
`pnr` (see [the overview of LPR join keys](understand-lpr.qmd)). A value that
is measured **relative to the index date** (socioeconomic position, a
comorbidity score) is joined on `pnr` + `index_date`, so it still lands on the
right row when the same person is in the cohort with more than one index date.
The ER diagram below shows both - extracts joined onto the cohort:

```{mermaid}
erDiagram
    full_cohort ||--o| extract_hip_fracture : "pnr"
    full_cohort ||--o| extract_ses : "pnr + index_date"
    full_cohort ||--o| extract_nmi : "pnr + index_date"
    full_cohort {
        string pnr PK
        date index_date PK
        int exposed
        string sex
        date foed_dag
    }
    extract_hip_fracture {
        string pnr FK
        date event_date
    }
    extract_ses {
        string pnr FK
        date index_date FK
        string education_cat
        string occupation_cat
        string income_cat
    }
    extract_nmi {
        string pnr FK
        date index_date FK
        int nmi
    }
```

The key is marked PK (primary key) in the cohort and FK (foreign key) in each
extract. The symbol `||--o|` is standard ER notation ("crow's foot"): `||` =
exactly one, `o|` = zero or one. So the line reads: each person in the cohort
matches **zero or one** row in the extract.

This describes the **shape you must ensure before the join** - not something
`left_join()` checks or fixes. If an extract has several rows per `pnr`,
`left_join()` happily proceeds and duplicates the cohort rows (row explosion).
That is why the callout above tells you to get each extract down to one row per
person *first*, and why check 1 in [Validate your join](#validate-your-join)
afterwards (did the row count grow?).

### The joins you will use

```r
library(dplyr) # left_join, inner_join, semi_join, anti_join

# left_join: keep ALL rows from x, add columns from y
# Persons in x without a match in y get NA.
result <- cohort %>%
  left_join(outcome, by = "pnr") # all cohort members retained; outcome = NA if no event

# inner_join: keep only rows with a match in BOTH tables
result <- lpr_adm %>%
  inner_join(lpr_diag, by = "recnum") # only contacts with at least one diagnosis

# right_join: keep all rows from y (rarely used)
# full_join: keep all rows from both (rarely used)
```

### Filter joins - change rows only, not columns

```r
# semi_join: keep rows in x THAT HAVE a match in y
bef_in_cohort <- bef %>%
  semi_join(cohort, by = "pnr") # only BEF rows for cohort members

# anti_join: keep rows in x THAT DO NOT HAVE a match in y
bef_not_in_cohort <- bef %>%
  anti_join(cohort, by = "pnr") # only BEF rows for non-cohort members
# also used for diagnostics - see "Validate your join" below
```

<details>
<summary>Overview: all joins in one table</summary>

| Function | Keeps rows from | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `left_join(x, y)` | All from x | Add outcomes/covariates to cohort - NA if no match |
| `inner_join(x, y)` | Only matches in both | Join contacts and diagnoses - only want rows with both |
| `right_join(x, y)` | All from y | Rarely |
| `full_join(x, y)` | All from both | Rarely |
| `semi_join(x, y)` | Only x with match in y | Filter a register to only cohort members |
| `anti_join(x, y)` | Only x without match in y | Find everyone in BEF NOT in the cohort |

</details>

### Join with multiple keys

Multiple keys only become relevant when **at least one of the tables has several
rows per person** - otherwise `pnr` alone is enough. With multiple keys **all**
the listed columns must agree before two rows count as a match (`pnr` *and*
`year`, not `pnr` *or* `year`).

The typical case is **panel data: registers with one row per person per year**.
BEF, AKM, FAIK and so on have a `pnr` row for every calendar year. Join two of
them on `pnr` alone and each of the person's rows is paired with *all* of the
person's rows in the other table: with 5 years in BEF and 5 in AKM you get every
combination, 5 × 5 = 25 rows instead of 5. Add the year as an extra key and
those 25 are filtered down to the 5 where the year also matches - 2018 against
2018:

```r
# Join on pnr AND year: a row matches only when BOTH columns are equal
bef_akm <- bef %>%
  left_join(akm, by = c("pnr", "year")) # 2018 BEF joins only to 2018 AKM
```

If instead you join two extracts that each have **one row per person** (e.g.
finished person-level extracts onto the cohort), `pnr` alone is enough - there
is no extra dimension to keep track of.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not assume "one row per person per year" - check it.** BEF on DARTER does
contain duplicate `(pnr, year)` rows, and adding the year as a key does not save
you from those: a person with two 2018 rows still doubles. Count first, and
reduce to one row per person per year if you find any.

```r
# Are there duplicates? n > 1 means the same person appears twice in one year.
bef %>%
  count(pnr, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  count() %>%
  collect()

bef <- bef %>% distinct(pnr, year, .keep_all = TRUE) # keep one row per person-year
```

`left_join()` will not warn you. It just returns more rows than you started
with, which is why check 1 in [Validate your join](#validate-your-join) is to
compare `nrow()` before and after.
:::

## Validate your join {#validate-your-join}

Joins rarely fail with an error message - but they can produce silently wrong
results. Always check these three things after a `left_join()`:

```r
# Before join: what is nrow?
nrow(cohort) # e.g. 4,823

# Join:
cohort2 <- cohort %>% left_join(outcome, by = "pnr")

# Check 1: did the row count increase? Duplicated keys in outcome give extra rows.
nrow(cohort2) # should still be 4,823

# Check 2: how many got a match?
sum(!is.na(cohort2$event_date)) # number with outcome
sum(is.na(cohort2$event_date)) # number without - expected censored?

# Check 3: who did NOT match? (diagnostic - not necessarily an error)
missing <- anti_join(cohort, outcome, by = "pnr") # pnr's not found in outcome
nrow(missing) # 0 = all matched; > 0 = investigate
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**`anti_join()` as diagnostics** `anti_join(cohort, outcome, by = "pnr")`
returns the cohort members that are *not* found in the outcome table. Use it for
"who in my cohort has no death date record?" (all alive - expected) or "who is
missing from register X?" (unexpected - investigate).
:::

## Stack tables vertically - `bind_rows()`

`bind_rows()` and `left_join()` solve **two fundamentally different problems**:

  |                 | `bind_rows()`                            | `left_join()`                                   |
  | --------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
  | What it does    | Stacks tables **vertically** - adds rows | Combines tables **horizontally** - adds columns |
  | Requires        | That the columns have the same names     | That the tables share one common key column     |
  | Result          | More rows, same number of columns        | Same number of rows, more columns               |
  | Matches on key? | No - all rows from both tables           | Yes - match on `pnr` or other key               |
  | Typical use     | LPR2 + LPR3 → one combined register      | Link outcome or covariate to cohort table       |

`bind_rows()` is **not** a join. It does not look at `pnr` and does not match.
It simply places table 2's rows below table 1's rows - like pasting two Excel
sheets together vertically.

```r
# bind_rows: LPR2 and LPR3 have the same columns (pnr, date_contact, icd3)
# → stack them vertically into one combined diagnosis register
lpr2_dx # 45,000 rows - diagnoses up to March 2019
lpr3_dx # 32,000 rows - diagnoses from March 2019 onwards

all_dx <- bind_rows(lpr2_dx, lpr3_dx) # 77,000 rows - both periods combined
```

Columns missing in one table (e.g. a column that only exists in LPR3) are
automatically filled with `NA` for rows from the other table.

Counting diagnoses across this combined `all_dx`? Expect a jump around
2019-2020 that isn't a real change in disease occurrence - see
[why](understand-lpr.qmd#lpr3-spike).

::: {.callout-note}
**When do you use which?** `bind_rows()` - when you have **two versions of the
same register** (LPR2 + LPR3, exposed + comparators) and want to merge them into
one. `left_join()` - when you want to **attach a new variable** (outcome, date
of death, age) to your cohort table.
:::

<details>
<summary>Practical examples: join date of death and emigration to the cohort</summary>

`read_register()` requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers - see
[Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if you did not convert them
from SAS yourself.

**Date of death (DOD)**

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr) # %>%, semi_join(), left_join(), collect()
library(tibble) # tibble()

# Attach date of death (DOD) to the cohort -------------------------------------
# Cohort data from Phase 10. Keep only the columns that identify a row and the
# ones Phase 10 owns. The file also holds working columns from the matching
# (death_date, first_outcome_date ...); attach those fresh here, so no column
# ends up twice (death_date.x / death_date.y).
cohort <- readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds") %>%
  select(pnr, index_date, exposed, sex, foed_dag,
         any_of(c("match_id", "crossover_date"))) # any_of(): kept if the column exists

# Death dates from DOD:
dod <- read_register("dod") %>% # without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/dod/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%               # standardise column names
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%   # only the cohort's pnr's
  select(pnr, death_date = doddato) %>%   # rename doddato to death_date
  collect()                              # fetch into R

# Join: all cohort members retained; the living get death_date = NA
cohort <- cohort %>%
  left_join(dod, by = "pnr")       # attach death date - NA = still alive
```

**Emigration date (VNDS)**

Emigration censors just like death - the person leaves the study on the day they emigrate.
VNDS contains one row per migration event. Take the first exit **after the index
date**, not simply the first ever: a person may have left and come back, and an
exit *before* index censors nothing. Whether the person was resident at index at
all is decided in [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd#step-1).

```r
# Attach emigration date (VNDS) to the cohort ----------------------------------
# Emigration dates from VNDS:
vnds <- read_register("vnds") %>%              # without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/vnds/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%                       # standardise column names
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%   # only the cohort's pnr's
  filter(indud_kode == "U") %>%                  # "U" = udvandring/emigration (VNDS holds both in- and out-migration)
  select(pnr, haend_dato) %>%
  collect()

emigration <- cohort %>%                         # the cohort has pnr + index_date
  distinct(pnr, index_date) %>%                  # one row per person and index date
  left_join(vnds, by = "pnr", relationship = "many-to-many") %>% # several index dates x several exits per person is expected here
  filter(haend_dato > index_date) %>%            # only exits AFTER index - those are the ones that censor
  group_by(pnr, index_date) %>%                  # per person AND index date: the answer depends on the index date
  arrange(haend_dato) %>%                        # oldest date first
  slice(1) %>%                                   # first exit after that index date
  ungroup() %>%                                  # release grouping
  select(pnr, index_date, emigration_date = haend_dato) # rename haend_dato to emigration_date

# Join: all cohort members retained; non-emigrants get emigration_date = NA
cohort <- cohort %>%
  left_join(emigration, by = c("pnr", "index_date")) # NA = no exit after index
```

The date of death is one date per person, so `pnr` alone is the right key. The
emigration date depends on the index date, so it is keyed on `pnr` **and**
`index_date`: a person who was drawn as a comparison person on two different
dates then gets the right exit for each of them.

</details>

## Derived variables: create new columns {#derived-variables-create-new-columns}

Once the extracts are joined, you almost always need to **compute new variables**
from the columns you now have. That is `mutate()`: it adds a column calculated
from existing ones.

```r
library(dplyr) # mutate, if_else, case_when

cohort <- cohort %>%
  mutate(
    # Age at index: days between two dates / 365.25 (a year is 365.25 days, leap years)
    age_at_index = as.numeric(index_date - foed_dag) / 365.25,

    # BMI from height (m) and weight (kg)
    bmi = weight_kg / (height_m^2),

    # Categorise a continuous variable into groups
    age_group = case_when(
      age_at_index < 50 ~ "<50",
      age_at_index < 65 ~ "50-64",
      TRUE ~ "65+" # everything else (here: 65 and over)
    )
  )
```

Two habits worth keeping:

- **Compute a variable once** and reuse it, so age at index is the same number in
  the matching and in Table 1.
- **`if_else()`** for yes/no, **`case_when()`** for several categories - and use
  the same type in every branch (`1L`/`0L`, or text in all of them). Both are in
  the [Function guide](function-guide.qmd).

The censoring date and the event indicator are derived variables too, but they
need dates from several extracts at once, so they come next.

## Calculate follow-up time and event variable {#follow-up-time}

Before you can analyse, each cohort member needs a **censoring date** (when
follow-up ends) and an **event variable** (did they experience the outcome?).

The censoring date is the *earliest* of: event date, date of death, emigration
date, the date a comparison person becomes exposed themselves (crossover) and
end of study period. `death_date` and `emigration_date` were joined on in the
practical examples above; the outcome date is joined on first here.

```r
# Calculate follow-up time and event variable ----------------------------------
# The outcome extract from Phase 9/11: pnr + event_date, one row per person
hip_fracture <- readRDS("path/to/extract_hip_fracture.rds") %>%
  distinct(pnr, event_date)
cohort <- cohort %>% left_join(hip_fracture, by = "pnr") # NA = no event

study_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31") # replace with your actual study end date
# format: "yyyy-mm-dd" (ISO 8601 - R's standard)

cohort <- cohort %>%
  mutate(
    # Censoring date = the earliest of all possible stopping reasons
    censor_date = pmin(
      event_date,
      death_date,
      emigration_date,
      crossover_date, # comparison person becomes exposed (NA for everyone else)
      study_end,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    # Follow-up time in days (Cox) and in years (rates, Poisson)
    time_days = as.numeric(censor_date - index_date),
    followup_years = time_days / 365.25,

    # Outcome variable: 1 = outcome occurred before censoring, 0 = censored
    outcome = as.integer(!is.na(event_date) & event_date <= censor_date)
  ) %>%
  filter(time_days > 0) # drop zero/negative follow-up (see below)
```

::: {.callout-note}
`pmin()` compares vectors position by position and returns the smallest value
per person - it is the vectorised version of `min()`. `na.rm = TRUE` ensures
that a missing death date (= alive) does not make the censoring date `NA`.
:::

**Crossover.** A comparison person who later becomes exposed stops being a
comparison person on that day, so follow-up is censored at `crossover_date`
(made in [Phase 10](comparison-cohort.qmd), `NA` for the exposed and for
comparison persons who never become exposed). Without that line, time after
their own exposure is counted as unexposed time. If your cohort has no
`crossover_date` column (no comparison group, or one that can never become
exposed), leave the line out. The alternative to censoring is to let the person
**switch group** at crossover and contribute exposed time from then on. That
needs a dataset with several rows per person, see [Time-varying
exposure](time-varying.qmd).

**Zero or negative follow-up.** Someone whose outcome, death or emigration is
recorded on the index date itself gets `time_days = 0` and was never at risk;
an event *before* index (a prevalent case that slipped through) gives a negative
time. Both break the analysis (`log(0)` in Poisson, meaningless Cox time), so
the `filter()` above drops them - count how many, and if same-day events are
common in your data, decide deliberately whether they belong in the study.

**Competing risks?** If a competing event (typically death) must be handled
separately (see [Time-to-event](time-to-event.qmd#competing-risks)),
then instead of a binary `outcome` (0/1) build a **status with three values** -
what happened *first*:

```r
# Competing risks: a status with three values ----------------------------------
cohort <- cohort %>%
  mutate(
    # status_code: which date "won" the pmin() above?
    status_code = case_when(
      !is.na(event_date) & event_date <= censor_date ~ 1, # outcome first
      !is.na(death_date) & death_date <= censor_date ~ 2, # death first (competing risk)
      TRUE ~ 0 # otherwise censored (emigration/study end)
    )
  )
```

## Assemble the final analysis dataset

By now your **cohort** is built in [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd): a
table with `pnr` and `index_date` (and `exposed`/`case` if
you have a comparison group - renamed to `exposure` in the final `select()`) - one row per **person**, unless your comparison
group was matched **with replacement**, in which case the same `pnr` can carry
several rows, one per `index_date` it was matched on. The recipe below works
for both: everything measured relative to the index date is joined on `pnr` +
`index_date`, see [comparison cohort's callout on
it](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-4---assemble-validate-and-save). Your **outcomes, covariates and censoring variables**
are extracted as separate RDS files ([Phase 9](extract-from-lpr.qmd), [Phase
11](extract-variables.qmd)). This last step joins them onto the cohort with
`left_join()`, calculates follow-up time, and keeps only the columns the
analysis needs.

::: {.callout-note}
**Cohort construction - including the matching - belongs to [Phase
10](build-study-population.qmd).** Here we assume the cohort already exists;
this page only assembles the analysis dataset around it. Design choices
(comparator, immortal time, matching ratio) are decided back in [Phase
1](plan-your-study.qmd#comparator-cohort).
:::

::: {.callout-important}
**End with `select()` - keep only the columns the analysis requires.**

```r
cohort_final <- cohort %>%
  select(
    pnr,
    index_date,
    exposure = exposed, # renamed: the analysis pages call it `exposure`
    censor_date,
    time_days,
    followup_years,
    outcome,
    status_code, # from the competing-risks block above
    age, # age, nmi and the three _cat columns are added in the
    sex, # complete recipe below (steps 4 and 5)
    nmi,
    occupation_cat,
    education_cat,
    income_cat
  )

saveRDS(cohort_final, "path/to/analysis.rds") # save the final dataset
```
:::

<details>
<summary>Complete recipe - from cohort to analysis-ready dataset</summary>

```r
# Complete recipe: cohort -> analysis-ready dataset ----------------------------
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr)   # left_join, semi_join, mutate, group_by, slice
library(tibble)  # tibble()

# 0. Load your cohort ----------------------------------------------------------
# One row per person and index date. Keep only the columns that identify a row
# and the ones Phase 10 owns; everything else is attached fresh below, so no
# column ends up twice (death_date.x / death_date.y).
cohort <- readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds") %>%
  select(pnr, index_date, exposed, sex, foed_dag,
         any_of(c("match_id", "crossover_date"))) # any_of(): kept if the column exists
n_start <- nrow(cohort)   # to check below that no join adds or loses rows

# THE JOIN KEY. A date that belongs to the person (outcome, death) is joined on
# pnr. Anything measured RELATIVE TO THE INDEX DATE (emigration after index, SES,
# NMI) is joined on pnr + index_date: with a comparison group matched with
# replacement the same pnr has several rows, one per index date, and a join on
# pnr alone would then silently multiply the rows.

# 1. Prevalent cases are already excluded --------------------------------------
# People who already had the outcome before index are not at risk of getting it.
# They were removed in Phase 10 (build-study-population.qmd, Step 3: the
# `prevalent` object and filter(!pnr %in% prevalent)), so full_cohort.rds holds
# only people at risk at index. The filter in step 4 catches any that slipped through.

# 2. Link the outcome ----------------------------------------------------------
# One row per person with the FIRST event date after index, or no row at all.
# left_join keeps everyone, so people with no event get NA - which is exactly
# what "no event" means here, and what the outcome indicator in step 4 reads.
hip_fracture <- readRDS("path/to/extract_hip_fracture.rds") %>%   # pnr + event_date
  distinct(pnr, event_date)                                       # one row per person
cohort <- cohort %>% left_join(hip_fracture, by = "pnr")

# 3. Link censoring: death date and emigration ---------------------------------
deaths <- read_register("dod") %>%   # without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/dod/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  select(pnr, death_date = doddato) %>% collect()

vnds_data <- read_register("vnds") %>%    # without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/vnds/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  filter(indud_kode == "U") %>%
  select(pnr, haend_dato) %>% collect()

# Emigration needs the first exit AFTER index, not the first ever: someone who
# lived abroad as a child and moved back is not censored at that childhood exit.
# So attach index_date first, filter, and only then take the earliest remaining,
# per person AND index date.
vnds_data <- cohort %>%
  distinct(pnr, index_date) %>%
  left_join(vnds_data, by = "pnr", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%   # several index dates x several exits per person is expected
  filter(haend_dato > index_date) %>%
  group_by(pnr, index_date) %>% arrange(haend_dato) %>% slice(1) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(pnr, index_date, emigration_date = haend_dato)

cohort <- cohort %>%
  left_join(deaths,    by = "pnr") %>%
  left_join(vnds_data, by = c("pnr", "index_date"))

stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == n_start)   # a join that multiplied rows stops here

# 4. Follow-up time and the outcome indicator ----------------------------------
# censor_date = the FIRST of the ways follow-up can end. pmin() with
# na.rm = TRUE takes the earliest date that actually exists, so someone who never
# died, never emigrated and never had the event simply ends at study_end.
# crossover_date = the day a comparison person becomes exposed themselves (from
# Phase 10; NA for everyone else). Leave that line out if your cohort has no such column.
# outcome = 1 only if the outcome happened at or before that date: a diagnosis
# recorded after the person emigrated does not count. status_code adds death as
# a competing event (0 = censored, 1 = outcome, 2 = death; outcome wins a tie).
study_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31")   # replace with your actual study end date (the last date your data cover)
cohort <- cohort %>%
  mutate(
    censor_date    = pmin(event_date, death_date, emigration_date, crossover_date,
                          study_end, na.rm = TRUE),
    time_days      = as.numeric(censor_date - index_date),
    followup_years = time_days / 365.25,   # 365.25 = leap years
    outcome        = as.integer(!is.na(event_date) & event_date <= censor_date),
    status_code    = case_when(
      outcome == 1 ~ 1,
      !is.na(death_date) & death_date <= censor_date ~ 2,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    age            = as.numeric(index_date - foed_dag) / 365.25   # age at index, for every row
  ) %>%
  filter(time_days > 0)   # no follow-up = never at risk (event/death/emigration on index day)

# 5. Link covariates (SES, comorbidity) ----------------------------------------
# sex and age are already on the cohort (step 0 and step 4). The extracts below
# are measured relative to the index date, so they are joined on pnr + index_date.
# distinct() makes sure each extract has ONE row per key: the same person can be
# drawn into two matched sets on the same date, and two identical rows on each
# side would otherwise become four.
ses_data <- readRDS("path/to/extract_ses.rds") %>%    # education_cat, occupation_cat, income_cat
  distinct(pnr, index_date, .keep_all = TRUE)
nmi_data <- readRDS("path/to/extract_nmi.rds") %>%    # NMI score - see nmi.qmd
  distinct(pnr, index_date, .keep_all = TRUE)

n_before <- nrow(cohort)
cohort <- cohort %>%
  left_join(ses_data, by = c("pnr", "index_date")) %>%
  left_join(nmi_data, by = c("pnr", "index_date"))
stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == n_before)   # same number of rows as before the joins

# 6. Keep ONLY the columns the analysis requires -------------------------------
cohort_final <- cohort %>%
  select(pnr, index_date, exposure = exposed, censor_date, time_days, followup_years,
         outcome, status_code, age, sex, nmi, occupation_cat, education_cat, income_cat)

saveRDS(cohort_final, "path/to/analysis.rds")  # save the final dataset
nrow(cohort_final)   # n_start minus the rows dropped for zero follow-up in step 4
names(cohort_final)  # did every join actually add the columns you expected?
```

</details>

## Next steps

You now have one analysis-ready dataset with one row per person (one row per
person and index date, if your comparison group was matched with replacement). The next step
is the analysis:

→ [Phase 13 - Analysis](analysis.qmd)
